newsitem.title: UK: UK's Thatcher misses power but rules out comeback.
newsitem.headline: UK's Thatcher misses power but rules out comeback.

text.p: Former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher said on Sunday it was hard to kick the habit of being in charge but ruled out a comeback.

In what was billed as her only interview before Britain elects its next prime minister on May 1, Thatcher showed all her old grasp of detail when quizzed about the forthcoming election, but turned wistful when she recalled her own days at the helm.
"I got so used to being in charge that it takes a long time to get out of an old habit," Thatcher told the Sunday Telegraph seven years after saying goodbye to Downing Street.
Britain's longest serving premier of the century was ousted by her own party and many Britons have wondered if the Iron Lady -- a woman who clearly savoured power -- might stage a comeback.
The arch-conservative, still vigorous and intellectually formidable at 71, denied she hankered after high office.

"I have no wish to come back. Now I am free to roam the world and preach my beliefs -- and I am having an effect," said Thatcher, who gives speeches at home and abroad and runs an institute propagating her free-market beliefs.
Dubbed "nanny to the nation" for her badgering tone while in office and her stridency in running government, Thatcher was both reviled and respected for her tough, no-nonsense style.

In office -- she was there for 11 years -- Thatcher put in an 18-hour day, ate and drank little, and reluctantly consented to take one week's holiday a year. A workaholic, she had no interests outside politics and power.

Since losing office, Thatcher has remained an influential voice in British politics, sniping at her party from the sidelines and often upstaging her chosen heir, Prime Minister John Major, with her outspoken views.
On overseas tours, Thatcher receives star treatment and remains better known than Major, dubbed the grey man of politics.
Indeed, Thatcher has often damned her chosen successor with faint praise but she used the interview to voice support for "honest John" Major in his struggle to win re-election.
As for the general election itself -- she has won three of them -- Thatcher was characteristically opinionated.
The campaign was too long and too boring, the idea of presidential-style debates was silly and the import of U.S.-style gimmicks on the stump was to be deplored.

"Three weeks (of campaigning) is quite long enough, otherwise people get bored. And anyway, it's the last week that counts. That's when you can really change things," said Thatcher, who only began actively campaigning for the Conservatives in the past week, half-way through the campaign.

As for the woman herself, some things haven't changed a jot since the heady days of the 1980s when she transformed Britain with her creed of Thatcherism, according to the interviewer -- her former private secretary Sir Charles Powell.
"The voice and manner have not changed. All the vigour and energy which carried her to victory in three elections are as much in evidence as ever," he wrote.
"The lasting impression remains of a battleship called back into service among a fleet of frigates...She still leaves the rest of the political establishment dead in the water."
